idiom_name: list/set/dict comprehension, generator expression, built-in map()
implementation_notes: Python has no map on its containers, so the operation appears as syntax or as a builtin: a list/set/dict comprehension applies a transformation per element and materialises, a generator expression does the same lazily, and the built-in map(function, iterable) returns a lazy iterator that applies the function to every item and must be consumed. For the absent-value context there is no container to map over - the equivalent is the conditional expression written where the value is used (f(x) if x is not None else None), or a library container if the team wants the named operation. Comprehensions replace the classic structure and functools.reduce is the terminal; keep map() when a named or built-in function already exists and a lambda would only add noise.
code_sketch:
names = [p.display_name for p in people]        # eager list comprehension
lazy = (p.display_name for p in people)        # generator expression
ports = list(map(int, raw_ports))              # builtin, lazy until list()

# no Maybe container: the absent case stays a conditional expression
host = cfg.host if cfg is not None else None
pitfalls: A list comprehension materialises while a generator expression is single-use: consuming the same generator twice silently yields nothing the second time.
The built-in map is lazy, so map(f, xs) alone does nothing, and a map object has no length or indexing - list() or iteration is the terminal.
None is not a context: there is no x.map(f), so the absent case is restated as a conditional at every site, which is exactly where a value gets dropped inconsistently.

variants.name: returns containers (Maybe / Result / IO) with .map
variants.implementation_notes: When the codebase genuinely wants named contexts - a value that may be absent, a computation that may fail - dry-python's returns supplies them with the operation attached: the documentation defines Maybe.map(function) as composing the container with a pure function (Some('a').map(lambda s: s + 'b') == Some('ab')) and leaving Nothing unchanged, and Result/IO/Requirement carry the same method, so pipelines can be written once against the container types. This is the closest Python gets to an instance declaration, with bind/apply above it and law-checked containers below. It replaces ad-hoc None and exception plumbing but adds a dependency and container types the rest of the ecosystem (including type-checker narrowing) does not know, so it is a codebase-wide decision rather than a local one.
variants.code_sketch:
from returns.maybe import Maybe
from returns.result import Result

display: Maybe[str] = Maybe.from_optional(user).map(lambda u: u.display_name)
port: Result[int, ValueError] = Result.from_value(raw).map(int)
# Nothing and Failure pass through untouched: map never sees them
pitfalls: The containers are library types: type checkers narrow plain T | None, not Maybe, so mypy/pyright flows need the project's conventions applied consistently or the gain is lost.
Wrapping values that cannot be absent or cannot fail adds indirection; the guidance is Maybe for absence and Result for expected failures, not a container around every value.

Mixing containers with raw None and exceptions at the boundary re-creates the plumbing the container was meant to remove, so the boundary is where the container is created and destroyed - nothing in between.
